title: The Italian Connection
subtitle: From Sanremo and Cinecittà to the Warehouse

steps.text: Post-war Italy's popular song borrows opera's melodic sweep: verses that climb to a held note, arrangements for full orchestra, and a national festival — Sanremo — to launch them.
The same Rome studios score films. Morricone arranges Mina and Gino Paoli by day and, from 1964, turns the western into whistling, twang and choir.
By the late 70s, DJs at lakeside clubs pitch disco records down into slow, hypnotic blends — Italy's first dancefloor invention.
Then disco's money disappears. Milan producers keep the chorus, drop the orchestra and sequence everything — cheap, glossy, melodic records for export.
Those exports land in Chicago. Knuckles and Hardy loop the basslines; the first house records inherit Italo's sequenced octave bass.

title: Antiquity to the Concert Hall
subtitle: 2,400 years from the aulos to functional harmony

steps.text: It starts with a single line: voice doubled by lyre or aulos, shaped by poetic meter. No chords, no harmony — but a theory of tetrachords and named modes that will outlive the civilisation.
The medieval church inherits those modes, renames them, and sings them unaccompanied. To preserve the repertoire it invents the staff — and Europe gains a way to write music down.
Voices are added against the chant line. Once several move at once, consonance between them becomes a rule, and the triad settles in as the resting sound.
Around 1600 the equal voices are set aside. One singer carries the drama over a bass line and chords — melody plus accompaniment, staged with an orchestra, and the words are audible again.
Counterpoint hardens into functional harmony: keys, cadences, long-range tonal structure, and notated forms built to carry them.
By 1900 that tonal system is exhausted enough to break. Impressionism, atonality and serialism dismantle the very grammar antiquity set in motion.
And the reaction to that break loops back: repetition, static modal centres and an unmeasured line — chant's logic, rebuilt from the other end of history.

title: Hardcore to the Emo Revival
subtitle: Punk's fury turned inward, four decades on

steps.text: Punk compresses rock into fast, confrontational, DIY bursts — the raw material.
American hardcore strips it further: faster, shorter, angrier, and fiercely self-organised.
In D.C.'s 1985 Revolution Summer, Rites of Spring and Embrace turn that fury inward — emotional hardcore.
Post-hardcore keeps the intensity but opens the form — dynamics, dissonance and space.
The mid-90s second wave makes emo confessional and melodic.
In Midwest basements it relaxes into twinkly, math-inflected intimacy — American Football's porch light.
A 2010s generation raised on those records brings the lineage back, group-shouts and all.

title: Blues to Rock 'n' Roll
subtitle: How the blues was electrified for teenagers

steps.text: It begins with the blues — the 12-bar cycle, blue notes and call-and-response that underpin everything that follows.
Migration north and amplification turn it into Chicago blues: a loud, band-driven sound with a distorted, sustaining guitar tone.
Given a hard backbeat and horns, it becomes rhythm & blues — urban, danceable and built for the jukebox.
Sped up and aimed at teenagers, R&B's shuffle becomes rock 'n' roll, with Chuck Berry codifying the electric-guitar language.
Post-punk's cold, cavernous space proves guitars can evoke vast atmosphere, not just aggression.
Dream pop warms that space — Cocteau Twins and Mazzy Star drown breathy melody in shimmering reverb.
In parallel, noise pop buries sweet pop hooks under feedback, making the noise itself melodic.
Shoegaze fuses both into a single overwhelming wall of glide-guitar texture, perfected on My Bloody Valentine's Loveless.
Disco lays the foundation: four-on-the-floor, the extended 12-inch mix and a club culture born in queer and Black spaces.
When disco falls from fashion, Chicago DJs keep it alive with drum-machine edits — proto-house.
Those edits become original productions. The 909 kick and soul samples crystallise into house.
Larry Heard turns house inward, adding lush jazz chords and a subdued warmth: deep house.

title: Jazz to Fusion to Spillover
subtitle: How jazz seeded the experimental fringe

steps.text: Bebop reclaims jazz as virtuoso art music — fast, harmonically dense improvisation over rapid changes.
Modal jazz replaces those changes with open, scale-based vamps, trading density for hypnotic space.
Plugged into rock's volume and backbeat, jazz becomes fusion — electric, aggressive and exploratory.
That electric, exploratory spirit echoes in krautrock, whose motorik repetition bridges rock, jazz and electronics.
At the far end, the experiment dissolves into ambient — beat and progression recede until only tone and drift remain.

title: Post-Punk to Dream Pop to Shoegaze
subtitle: The textural guitar lineage

steps.text: Post-punk opens guitar music into cold, dub-treated space and angular, bass-led arrangements.
Dream pop warms that space into lush reverb, blurring vocal and guitar into pure mood.
Shoegaze maximises the layering — glide guitar and buried vocals collapse into one overwhelming texture.
It starts with house: Chicago's soulful, sample-led four-on-the-floor, warm and song-like.
In Detroit, the same machines turn colder and futurist — funk syncopation rebuilt as machine soul.
Europe hardens Detroit's sound into relentless, metallic techno for big, dark rooms.
A melodic branch splits off into trance — sequenced arpeggios and long builds engineered for euphoria.

title: The Roots of Jazz
subtitle: Ragtime to bebop in four moves

steps.text: It begins with ragtime — America's first syncopated popular music, a steady striding left hand under a 'ragged' right.
In New Orleans those rhythms meet the blues and collective horn improvisation, and jazz is born.
Arranged for big bands, jazz becomes swing — smooth four-to-the-bar dance music for the masses.
A small-group revolt against swing's polish, bebop reclaims jazz as fast, virtuosic art music.
Bebop's dense changes finally give way to modal jazz's open, scale-based space.

title: Garage to Psych to the Desert
subtitle: Sixties fuzz to nu-psych and the modern frontier

steps.text: It begins in suburban garages — teenage bands playing three distorted chords with attitude over polish.
The studio and the trip expand that raw fuzz into psychedelic rock: modal jams, drones and tape-effect exploration.
Acid rock is its heavier, jam-based end — San Francisco ballroom volume and ten-minute improvisations.
Heavy psych pushes it to physical extremes: saturated amp stacks and dragging riffs — the missing link toward metal.
Black Sabbath darkens and codifies that weight into heavy metal — the tritone riff as monolith.
Doom metal slows Sabbath's blueprint to a funereal crawl, keeping the riff sacred through the 80s underground.
In Palm Desert, punk kids raised on those doom riffs detune them at generator parties — desert rock: fuzzy, groove-heavy, sun-baked.
Sleep and company take the desert sound worldwide as stoner rock: monolithic Sabbath riffs at a heavy-lidded crawl.
In parallel, neo-psychedelia reworks the 60s haze through indie sensibilities — Tame Impala's generation of nu-psych.
The 2020s frontier strips it back to velocity: desert punk, generator-party fuzz played at hardcore speed.

title: The 2026 Frontier
subtitle: Where the lineages are heading now

steps.text: Deep house's warm jazz chords travel south, to the townships of South Africa.
There they become amapiano — those chords floating over a springy log-drum bassline, the dominant global dance pulse of the 2020s.
Meanwhile spiritual jazz's modal, devotional vamps are picked up half a world away.
London's club-jazz scene reforges them as a new spiritual jazz, charged with Afro-diasporic rhythm and broken beat.
And post-punk's angular, bass-led tension proves it never really left.
It returns in the 2020s guitar-band revival — wry, literary and motorik, the lineage still evolving into 2026.

title: How Noir Crooner Emerged
subtitle: From Sinatra and doo-wop to Dead Man’s Bones

steps.text: It starts with the crooners. Sinatra leaves the Dorsey band in 1942 and the singer becomes the star; by 1955 In the Wee Small Hours is a whole album of late-night ballads.
On the R&B side, doo-wop groups fix the slow-dance ballad: I–vi–IV–V changes, a falsetto lead and, on The Flamingos' 'I Only Have Eyes for You', a haze of echo.

Roy Orbison starts at Sun Records in 1956 cutting rockabilly. At Monument he slows down and joins both lines: an operatic croon over doo-wop backing voices and strings on 'Only the Lonely', 'Crying' and 'In Dreams'.
Two decades later a darker branch comes out of Melbourne. Nick Cave's Birthday Party bend rockabilly and blues into violent post-punk noise.
When the band splits in 1983, Cave carries on as Nick Cave & the Bad Seeds: a baritone crooning murder ballads in a gothic setting.

In 1989 Chris Isaak's 'Wicked Game' puts Orbison's falsetto and tremolo guitar into that same dark mood. Dead Man's Bones (2009) add a children's choir and ghost stories, and Marlon Williams (from 2015) takes the croon back toward country.

title: How Witch House Emerged
subtitle: Houston tape culture meets goth electronics

steps.text: In early-90s Houston, DJ Screw drags rap tapes down to roughly 60% speed — pitch and tempo alone become the remix.
Elsewhere, goth's atmosphere had already left the band behind: darkwave carries minor-key dread on synths and drum machines.
Ethereal wave supplies the other half of the voice — wordless soprano dissolved in cathedral reverb.
Around 2009 bedroom producers fuse the two. Salem and Crystal Castles set screwed, unintelligible vocals over blown-out drum machines, and blogs name it witch house.
The micro-genre burns out within a few years, but its slowed, cavernous production keeps resurfacing in alternative R&B and pop.
